rv.q: With dazzling imagination and sublime control, the show’s cast and crew conjure a delirious, dynamic, highly pettable world.
...audiences attending this accomplished production are in store for a vastly ... pleasurable journey.
Pi knows that the best stories prioritize possibility over probability.

Working in tandem during the second act, when teenage Pi is adrift in the ocean with only dangerous zoo animals to keep him company, those fantastical images and Abeysekera’s boisterous energy create moment after moment of theatrical magic.
In the theater, what matters most is what an audience feels, what it cares about.
Visual appeal can’t quite wash away a stacked-deck ending, or make a convincing case for the fanciful over the plausible. Deep down, Mr. Okamoto probably agrees.
It’s a pity that he’s stranded in a story awash with platitudes.
As such, the production is more striking than stimulating.
Webster's stagecraft is dazzling, but don't expect Life of Pi to make you believe in God.

Spellbinding, enchanting, horrifying, staggering, epic, of the romance of life, of survival and family and faith, all of this and more is the Life of Pi now mesmerizing audiences on Broadway at the Theatre.
When a thrilling story finds a comparably thrilling scenic form, including all the marvels of lights, projections, and sound, theatre magic is created.
Mr. Webster and his team have risen to the occasion, lending vivid theatricality to a story that is, at its core, about faith and belief.

Whether or not his fantastical tale of sharing a lifeboat with a Bengal tiger for 227 days on the open seas will “make you believe in God,” as the 17-year-old shipwreck survivor named Pi Patel promises, the stage adaptation of Yann Martel’s best-selling novel “Life of Pi” will give you faith in the power of puppetry and in the magic of stagecraft….
Life of Pi is a show that succeeds on virtually every level, from its stunning visual effects to its deeply moving story about faith, survival, and the power of storytelling itself.
Visually, the play is a deeply wondrous spectacle that teems with beauty and brutality.
Like them, Life of Pi does a phenomenal job of creating a sense of realism with extraordinary stagecraft.
Abeysekera turns out to be just as good a reason to see the visually enchanting Life of Pi as the puppets.

The play feels somewhat drawn out at 135 minutes (including intermission), and the climactic narrative twist is too blatantly spoon-fed to the audience, as if the show’s creators were afraid that we would not be able to figure it out. But those are minor quibbles about this enthralling, wildly imaginative production.

‘Life of Pi’ is a most impressive and well-executed piece of theater...one suspects that the artists that brought the tiger and the other animals and visual effects to life will be deservedly recognized.
Whatever is or isn’t true about what happened to Pi, what resonates is an act of colorful imagining—and Richard Parker’s menacing roar.
Life of Pi is a unique theatrical experience with its animal puppetry, depiction of 227 days on the ocean, and bringing to life an Indian city, circa 1977.
Bring the kids, bring the edibles, and prepare to have your ship gently rocked.
It's a peculiar production, staged with tremendous brio yet never as engaging as one might hope.

In Chakrabarti’s pedestrian adaptation, when Pi (Hiran Abeysekera) is trapped on the boat with the hyena, the rat, the ape and the zebra (the tiger is still floating around in the ocean at this point in the story), you don’t worry that the boy might be attacked or eaten by the hyena.
Sadly, though, the show's breathtaking visual effects prove to be the best reason to see this otherwise unimpressive adaptation of Yann Martel's best-selling novel.
Life of Pi is the rare Broadway experience these days that refuses to pander to its audience, instead telling a story of hope, resilience, and survival.
It delivers in a way that must be seen to be believed, as the stage moves, flows, opens, and emotes in the most astounding of ways, leaving you tantalized at almost every turn.
Also, in lieu of CGI, this version relies on stagecraft to visualize the water, the weather, and the wildlife—and it’s done with great imagination and precision.
Onstage puppeteers skillfully manipulate all these creatures and although the humans are always visible, the effect is often magical.

cn.t: Critics praise the spectacular puppetry and visual stagecraft as landmark achievements, though some find the emotional depth doesn't match the technical brilliance. Hiran Abeysekera's lead performance impresses across the board.

vs.sum: The Gerald Schoenfeld Theatre offers good sightlines with minimal obstructions, although some side seats may have partial views. The sound quality is generally strong, enhancing the theatrical experience. However, the seating is tight, which can affect comfort, particularly for taller patrons. The theater's ambiance is charming with its historic character, and while facilities are adequate, expect some lines at the bar and restrooms.

acc.note: 7 wheelchair spaces in Orchestra. Infrared devices available.
